The Work, Thought and Legacy of Rabbi Eliyah Shapira (the Eliyah Rabbah): A Comprehensive Study in History, Halakha and Bibliography
Historical Background, Life and Spiritual Environment
Rabbi Eliyah Shapira (5420, approximately 1660 – 8 Nisan 5472, 14 April 1712) stands as a central landmark in the halakhic and communal dynamics of Central European Jewry in the late 17th and early 18th centuries [cite: 1, 2]. His figure grew out of the most distinguished rabbinic elite in the city of Prague, which was at that time a foremost spiritual, scholarly and leadership center in the Holy Roman Empire and in the entire Bohemian-Ashkenazi region [cite: 1, 2]. His father, Rabbi Binyamin Wolf Shapira, served as a preacher and dayan in Prague, and was later appointed head of the community's rabbinic court and Rabbi of the Land of Bohemia, positions that gave the family a firm and influential standing of leadership [cite: 2, 3].
Rabbi Eliyah's youth was marked by Torah mobility between the centers of learning of Bohemia and Poland [cite: 1, 2, 3]. To broaden his studies he traveled to the city of Kalisz, where he acquired Torah from the great figures of his generation [cite: 1, 2, 3]. On his return to Prague he joined the community's framework of Torah and judicial leadership [cite: 2, 3]. Around the year 5448 (1688) he was appointed rabbi of the city of Kolín in Bohemia, a position he held until approximately 5455 (1694) [cite: 2]. After this period he returned to Prague and was appointed a dayan in the community's chief rabbinic court, called in the sources "Morei Shaveh" [cite: 2]. Around the year 5459 (1699) he received an approach from the community of Tykocin in Poland to serve as its rabbi, following the move of Rabbi Aryeh Leib Sirkis to Kraków [cite: 2]. In research and in Torah literature there is a historical dispute over whether he accepted the invitation and actually served there for a short period before returning to Prague, or whether he preferred to decline the offer and remain in the scholarly center of Prague [cite: 2]. In Prague he served, alongside his role as dayan, also as head of a yeshiva ("rosh metivta") and as the official preacher of the community [cite: 2, 3].
The family environment of Rabbi Eliyah Shapira reflected the Torah and social network of connections of the leadership of his generation [cite: 2, 3]. His brother-in-law, his father's son-in-law, was the Gaon Rabbi Yaakov Reischer, author of the halakhic and responsa literature "Chok Yaakov," "Shevut Yaakov" and "Minchat Yaakov" [cite: 3]. His wife, Dabrish (who died in 5485), was the daughter of R. Azriel Yom Tov Bondi, one of the leaders of Prague [cite: 2]. His children continued the dynasty of rabbis and public service [cite: 2]: his son Rabbi Aryeh Leib served as av beit din of Leipnik and died in his father's lifetime in 5472 [cite: 2]; his son Rabbi Shmuel later served as av beit din of Prague [cite: 2]; his son R. Shimon was one of the leaders of Prague Jewry and married the daughter of R. Binyamin Wolf, son of Rabbi Aharon Shimon Shapira [cite: 2]; and his daughter Rivka married R. Wolf Segal Frankel, son of Rabbi Issachar Berman Segal Frankel, author of "Matteh Yissachar" [cite: 2]. Rabbi Eliyah Shapira died in the prime of his years, in his father's lifetime, at only about 52, on 8 Nisan 5472 (1712), and was buried in the ancient Jewish cemetery of Prague [cite: 2, 3].
Stage of His Life | Approximate Date / Year | Role and Historical Significance
Birth in Prague | 5420 (approx. 1660) | Growing up in the Torah and leadership elite of Bohemian Jewry [cite: 1, 2]
Studies in Kalisz | The early 5440s | Acquiring Torah from Rabbi Avraham Abele Gombiner (author of the "Magen Avraham") [cite: 1, 2, 3]
Rabbinate of Kolín | 5448 (1688) – 5455 (1694) | First rabbinic post, in the community of Kolín in Bohemia [cite: 2]
Dayan and Head of Yeshiva in Prague | 5455 (1694) onward | Service as a dayan in the "Morei Shaveh" court, rosh metivta and preacher of the community [cite: 2]
Invitation to the Rabbinate of Tykocin | 5459 (1699) | Approach from the community of Tykocin in Poland (disputed whether he actually served there) [cite: 2]
Death | 8 Nisan 5472 (1712) | Death at a young age in his father's lifetime; buried in the ancient cemetery of Prague [cite: 2, 3]
His Teachers and Spiritual Influences
The Torah and halakhic teaching of Rabbi Eliyah Shapira was formed from a fusion of two central learning traditions of that period: the Polish halakhic-analytic tradition on the one hand, and the Ashkenazi-Bohemian beit midrash and customary tradition on the other [cite: 1, 2, 3, 4]. This fusion derived directly from the personality and authority of his foremost teachers [cite: 1, 2, 3].
His grandfather, his father's father, Rabbi Aharon Shimon Shapira (known in halakhic literature as the Maharash of Prague), served as mara d'atra, av beit din and rosh yeshiva in Prague, and was regarded as Rabbi Eliyah's foremost teacher [cite: 1, 2, 3]. Rabbi Eliyah frequently cites him in his works by the reverent epithet "my grandfather the Gaon," and from him adopted meticulous loyalty to the ancient customs of Prague and to the deeply rooted Ashkenazi halakhic ruling [cite: 2, 3, 4].
On the other hand, the period of his study in Kalisz with Rabbi Avraham Abele HaLevi Gombiner, author of the "Magen Avraham," shaped his analytic and corpus-oriented approach [cite: 1, 2, 3]. From the Magen Avraham he acquired the aspiration to investigate the sources of the law down to their foundations in the Talmud and in the words of the Rishonim, the demand for precision in the wording of the halakhic authorities, and the readiness to confront earlier authorities [cite: 1, 2, 5, 6]. In addition, in Prague he also studied with Rabbi Shmuel Helman, one of the city's important dayanim, who imparted to him the method of legal discussion practiced in the community's courts [cite: 2].
His Books and Works: The Philosophy of Interpretation of a Torah Enterprise
The literary enterprise of Rabbi Eliyah Shapira comprises halakhic works, Talmudic novellae and homiletical books [cite: 2, 3, 7]. The work "Eliyah Zuta" is a concise and condensed commentary that collects the main laws and comments on the books of the "Levush" of Rabbi Mordechai Yaffe ("Levush HaTekhelet" and "Levush HaChor," which parallel the Orach Chaim section of the Shulchan Arukh) [cite: 1, 2]. This book was printed in the author's lifetime in two editions in Prague (in 5449/1689 and in 5461/1701), and since then its text has been established as an integral part of the editions of the "Levush" [cite: 2].
His central and most influential work, "Eliyah Rabbah," was originally written as a broad, comprehensive and profound commentary on the books of the "Levush" [cite: 2, 3]. The work presents a detailed halakhic discussion, including extensive give-and-take with the words of the Rishonim and Acharonim, clarification of textual versions and a ruling of the halakha for practice [cite: 8]. The history of the work's printing was filled with historical vicissitudes [cite: 2, 3, 8, 9]: the work was not printed in the author's lifetime, and after his death his family members and students labored to bring it to print from copies [cite: 2, 3]. The author's original autograph manuscript was burned entirely in the great fire that consumed the Jewish Quarter of Prague in the year 5514 (1754), together with other manuscripts of the author [cite: 3, 8, 9]. The work was saved only thanks to a copy made in good time, which, according to the testimony of the publishers, was in part incomplete and blurred [cite: 3]. When bringing the work to print, the editors made a typographical decision to print the "Eliyah Rabbah" as a book arranged on the order of the "Shulchan Arukh" and not around the book of the "Levush" [cite: 2, 3]. This decision often caused misunderstanding among learners, since the precisions and critiques of the "Eliyah Rabbah" were originally directed at the wording of the "Levush" and not at the formulation of Maran the Shulchan Arukh [cite: 2, 3]. In modern editions the work has been restored to its original format and is printed alongside the books of the "Levush" or as an independent book under its own original opening words [cite: 2, 3].
Besides his halakhic works, Rabbi Eliyah Shapira composed a book of novellae and commentaries on tractates of the Babylonian Talmud, also called "Eliyah Rabbah," which was first printed by his grandson in Fürth in the year 5528 (1768) [cite: 2, 3, 7]. By virtue of his role as the community's preacher in Prague he also composed a book of sermons on the Torah, and he also left responsa on halakha, but these manuscripts went up in flames in the fire of Prague in the year 5514 and most of them were never published [cite: 2, 3, 8, 9].
Title of the Work | Subject and Genre | Format and Printing | Status and History of the Work
Eliyah Zuta | Short commentary on the Levush (Orach Chaim) | Printed in his lifetime (Prague 5449, 5461) [cite: 2] | Printed regularly in all editions of the "Levush" [cite: 2]
Eliyah Rabbah (on the Levush) | Broad commentary and halakhic ruling (Orach Chaim) | Printed after his death from a manuscript copy [cite: 2, 3] | The original was burned in 5514; mistakenly arranged on the Shulchan Arukh and from there into an independent book [cite: 2, 3, 8, 9]
Eliyah Rabbah (on the Talmud) | Novellae on tractates of the Talmud | Printed in Fürth 5528 (1768) [cite: 2, 3, 7] | Printed by his grandson from manuscripts that survived [cite: 2, 3, 7]
Book of sermons and responsa | Sermons on the Torah and responsa | In manuscript | Lost almost entirely in the fire of Prague in the year 5514 [cite: 3, 8, 9]
His Halakhic Method, His Approach to Study and Bibliographic Precision
The halakhic method of the author of the "Eliyah Rabbah" is characterized by a combination of profound analytic scholarship with a tendency toward practical and clear decision [cite: 8]. Intellectual independence is evident in his halakhic discussions: on the one hand, the work was written around the text of the "Levush" out of great appreciation for the codification enterprise of Rabbi Mordechai Yaffe [cite: 2]. On the other hand, the "Eliyah Rabbah" does not shrink from criticizing the "Levush" when he finds that the latter deviated from the ancient custom of Ashkenaz or from the ruling of the Gemara and the Rishonim [cite: 4, 5, 10]. Rabbi Eliyah displays a similar attitude toward his foremost teacher, the author of the "Magen Avraham" [cite: 1, 2, 5, 11]. In many cases he confronts the novellae of the Magen Avraham with references in the Rishonim or with the custom of Prague, and rules contrary to his teacher's words [cite: 5, 11, 12, 13].
One of the prominent hallmarks of the book "Eliyah Rabbah" is its exceptional bibliographic richness [cite: 8]. The Chida, in his book "Machazik Bracha," extolled it greatly and wrote that the "Eliyah Rabbah" searched in all the chambers of the libraries of the righteous and that all the books of the house of study are surveyed before him [cite: 8], and likewise the author of the "Chayei Adam" wrote in his introduction that the book is exceedingly honored because all the books of the Rishonim, and also many manuscripts, were before its author [cite: 8]. Nevertheless, over the years editors and learners have spoken out against what appeared to be many citation errors and incorrect references in the book, as the author of the "Chayei Adam" remarked in his time that the book contains many scribal errors [cite: 8].
A thorough bibliographic study printed in recent years proved that the notion of the "many printing errors" in the "Eliyah Rabbah" was fundamentally mistaken and stemmed from the bibliographic ignorance of modern editors regarding the exact editions and manuscripts that lay on Rabbi Eliyah Shapira's table at the end of the 17th century [cite: 8]. Rabbi Eliyah Shapira used rare first printed editions, which differ in their structure, in the numbering of their sections and in the division of their pages from the editions common today [cite: 8]:
The citations of Sefer Chasidim in the "Eliyah Rabbah," which appear more than 180 times, correspond exactly to the first edition (Bologna 5298), in which the numbering of the sections is entirely different from the later editions [cite: 8]. His references to the book Shibbolei HaLeket, brought more than 250 times, correspond to the first, abridged edition (Venice 5306), which was the only edition available in his time, and not to the edition of the "complete Shibbolei HaLeket" which was printed from manuscripts centuries later [cite: 8]. Similarly, the citations of Sefer Yereim correspond to the abridgment of Sefer Yereim (Venice edition 5326) that was common in his time, and not to the complete edition that was printed only at the end of the 19th century [cite: 8]. Likewise, the quotations of the responsa of the Maharil correspond to the Hanau edition (5370), in which the numbering of the sections was changed and errors were corrected according to manuscripts, and not to the Cremona editions [cite: 8]. Even the references to the book "Maadanei Melekh," which many editors hastened to "correct" to "Maadanei Yom Tov," are faithful to the work's original name before its name was changed by the author [cite: 8].
The Book Cited in the "Eliyah Rabbah" | The Edition Before the Author | The Gap from Today's Common Editions | Significance of the Bibliographic Discovery
Sefer Chasidim | First edition, Bologna 5298 (1538) [cite: 8] | Section numbering entirely different from the Margaliot editions [cite: 8] | The section references are entirely accurate according to the Bologna edition [cite: 8]
Shibbolei HaLeket | Venice edition 5306 (1546) [cite: 8] | The abridgment of Shibbolei HaLeket (the only one printed in his time) [cite: 8] | The references to pages and sections correspond exactly to this edition [cite: 8]
Sefer Yereim | Abridgment of Yereim, Venice edition 5326 (1566) [cite: 8] | The "complete Yereim" was printed only at the end of the 19th century [cite: 8] | The references correspond to the abridgment that was common in the 17th century [cite: 8]
Responsa of the Maharil | Hanau edition 5370 (1610) [cite: 8] | Section numbering differs from the Cremona edition of 5316 [cite: 8] | The references correspond to the corrected Hanau edition [cite: 8]
Maadanei Yom Tov | An earlier edition under the name "Maadanei Melekh" [cite: 8] | The later change of name by the author [cite: 8] | The original reference of the author of the "Eliyah Rabbah" was accurate for its time [cite: 8]
His Students, His Influence and His Legacy for the Generations
The students of Rabbi Eliyah Shapira in Prague carried the torch of his teaching after his death in his prime, labored over copying his manuscripts, and brought his work "Eliyah Rabbah" to the printing press [cite: 2, 3]. His books, and especially the book "Eliyah Rabbah," were received in the world of Torah and halakha with exceptional favor and became an enduring asset of Ashkenazi halakhic ruling [cite: 2, 3, 8].
The central halakhic authorities of the 18th and 19th centuries regarded the author of the "Eliyah Rabbah" as a decisive halakhic authority. The Chida in his books "Machazik Bracha" and "Shem HaGedolim" dealt with his method with great respect, noting his comprehensive mastery [cite: 8]; the author of the "Chayei Adam" based many discussions on him in the Orach Chaim section and regarded him as one of the fathers of halakhic instruction [cite: 8]; and eminent authorities such as the author of "Shulchan Arukh HaRav," the author of "Arukh HaShulchan" and the author of the "Kitzur Shulchan Arukh" frequently cited his rulings as the basis for the halakhic ruling accepted in the communities of Ashkenaz and Poland [cite: 14, 15, 16, 17, 18].
The peak of the influence of the "Eliyah Rabbah" can be seen in the book "Mishnah Berurah" of Maran Rabbi Yisrael Meir HaKohen of Radin [cite: 2, 3, 12, 14, 19]. The "Mishnah Berurah" regards the "Eliyah Rabbah" as one of the four central pillars of halakhic instruction in the Orach Chaim section among the Acharonim, alongside the Magen Avraham, the Taz and the Dagul MeRevavah [cite: 2, 3, 12, 14, 15]. In thousands of places throughout the work the "Mishnah Berurah" cites the ruling of the "Eliyah Rabbah," and frequently, when there is a dispute between the Taz and the Magen Avraham, the "Mishnah Berurah" chooses to rule like the position of the "Eliyah Rabbah," which served for it as a mediating and deciding factor in the Ashkenazi beit midrash [cite: 2, 3, 12, 13, 14, 15].
Summary and Conclusions
Rabbi Eliyah Shapira of Prague, author of the "Eliyah Rabbah," stands in the front rank of the Ashkenazi halakhic authorities at the transition from the 17th century to the 18th [cite: 1, 2]. His Torah leadership, which extended across Prague, Kolín and the expanses of Bohemia and Poland, uniquely fused the beit midrash learning tradition of Prague with the broad halakhic analysis of the Torah centers in Poland [cite: 1, 2, 3, 4].
His written enterprise, despite the heavy disaster of the burning of his manuscripts in the year 5514, left an indelible mark on the world of halakha [cite: 3, 8, 9]. His book "Eliyah Rabbah," originally written as a commentary on the "Levush," became, thanks to its depth, its mastery and its bibliographic comprehensiveness, a foundational book in halakhic ruling in Orach Chaim [cite: 2, 3, 8]. Modern bibliographic research completed the picture of the figure, proving that what was regarded for generations as a "printing error" in his work is nothing but testimony to his meticulousness and to his use of rare printed editions and manuscripts that lay before him [cite: 8]. His central standing in the halakhic works of the 19th and 20th centuries, and first and foremost in the book "Mishnah Berurah," ensures the place of the author of the "Eliyah Rabbah" as one of the fathers of Ashkenazi halakhic ruling throughout the generations [cite: 2, 3, 12, 14, 15, 19].
